papers.headline: Chinese lunar missions reconstruct the history of the Moon's biggest crater
papers.original_title: Postimpact evolution of the South Pole–Aitken basin revealed by Chang’e-4 and Chang’e-6
papers.reason: The first ground-truth samples from the Moon's far-side South Pole–Aitken basin date its giant impact to about 4.34 billion years ago and reconstruct how the basin evolved afterwards.
papers.summary:
The South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin, on the Moon's far side, is the largest impact crater on the Moon and holds a record of its early geological history. Until recently no spacecraft had landed there. China's Chang'e-4 rover, which studies rocks on the surface, and the Chang'e-6 mission, which brought samples back to Earth, supplied the first direct measurements from inside the basin. The authors used these ground-level data and samples to piece together how the basin changed after it formed.

They conclude that the giant SPA impact happened about 4.34 billion years ago and melted so much rock that it produced a thick layer of molten material. As this layer cooled, it separated into different rock types, including norites with a moderate magnesium content. These rocks are exposed at the basin's central peaks, and a later impact (Finsen) threw some of them to the area Chang'e-4 is now exploring in Von Kármán crater. The team also identified rocks very rich in magnesium, probably formed by a separate episode of magma activity known as the Mg-suite. These were first dug up by the Apollo impact about 4.2 billion years ago and later carried to the Chang'e-6 landing site by a smaller impact (Chaffee S). Further events, such as the Orientale impact about 3.87 billion years ago, continued to reshape the basin.
papers.why_it_matters: Because the SPA basin is so old and so deep, it can reveal how the early Moon formed its crust and how giant impacts and volcanic activity changed it. Measurements taken on the ground and in returned samples give a firmer check on ideas that previously rested mostly on observations from orbit.
papers.limitations: The abstract describes a reconstructed sequence built from data at only two landing sites, and some links, such as the Mg-rich rocks coming from Mg-suite magmatism, are described as likely rather than certain. The exact methods and uncertainties on the ages are not given in the abstract.

key_terms.meaning: A very large crater, often hundreds to thousands of kilometres wide, made when a big asteroid or comet hits a planet or moon.
A layer of rock melted by the heat of a large impact that fills the floor of the crater.
Separation of a cooling molten body into layers of different composition as different minerals crystallize.
A coarse-grained igneous rock made mostly of plagioclase feldspar and a magnesium- and iron-bearing mineral called pyroxene.
A group of ancient magnesium-rich lunar rocks thought to come from magma that rose into the early crust.
Mountains or rings of mountains inside large craters, formed when the floor rebounds after impact, often bringing up deep material.
Direct measurements on site, used to test conclusions drawn from remote observations.

papers.headline: Gut inflammation after a type of CAR T cell therapy often fails to resolve
papers.original_title: Multicenter characterization of enterocolitis associated with BCMA-directed CAR T cell therapy
papers.reason: A large multicenter case series shows that enterocolitis after BCMA CAR-T therapy often does not resolve and can be fatal, which matters directly for patient safety.
papers.summary:
CAR T cell therapy reprograms a patient's own immune cells to attack cancer. One version targets BCMA, a protein found on certain blood cells. This study asked what happens to patients who develop a serious inflammation of the intestines, called immune effector cell-associated enterocolitis, after receiving BCMA-directed CAR T cells. Researchers at several medical centers pooled cases into a large case series, a descriptive collection of patient records, to see how the condition behaved and how patients fared.

The condition was often persistent. By the most recent check-up, only about a third of affected patients (32%) had seen the enterocolitis clear up. Some patients died from complications that the researchers linked directly to this gut disorder.
papers.why_it_matters: CAR T cell therapies are used more and more, so doctors need to recognize their less familiar side effects. These results suggest that enterocolitis after BCMA-directed treatment can be long-lasting and sometimes fatal. That points to a need for better monitoring and treatment of this complication.
papers.limitations: This is a descriptive case series without a comparison group, so it shows how affected patients fared but cannot establish how common the condition is or what causes it. The summary available here gives no details on patient numbers, follow-up length, or treatments used.

key_terms.meaning: A treatment in which a patient's T cells (a type of immune cell) are engineered to carry a receptor that recognizes and attacks a chosen target on cancer cells.
A protein on the surface of certain blood cells, used as the target that the engineered T cells are directed against.
Inflammation of the small and large intestines.
Caused by or linked to the activity of immune cells given as therapy, here the CAR T cells.
A study that describes a group of patients with a particular condition, without a comparison group.

H., Song, J., Gonzalez, R., Shestakova, A., Chowla, N., Chen, Z. E., Godara, A., Mohyuddin, G. R., Brondfield, M. N., ... Wolf, J. L. (2026). papers.headline: Confined cobalt catalyst breaks down 'forever chemicals' without added energy
papers.original_title: Steering nanometric reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycle for PFAS mineralization
papers.reason: A confined single-atom cobalt catalyst breaks down 'forever chemical' PFAS completely without external energy input, offering a possible practical route to water remediation.
papers.summary:
PFASs, nicknamed 'forever chemicals', contain carbon–fluorine bonds so strong that ordinary water treatment cannot break them. Most methods that do destroy them need an outside energy source such as light, electricity or heat. The authors asked whether a chemical reaction alone could do the job if it were run inside extremely narrow spaces. They built a catalyst by placing isolated single cobalt atoms on MXene, a material made of very thin stacked sheets, and used it to activate peroxymonosulfate, an oxidizing chemical, in a Fenton-like cycle (a repeating metal-driven reaction that generates reactive radicals).

Inside the nanometre-scale gaps between the sheets, one radical type (SO5•−) was protected from being destroyed by other substances in the water and stayed active long enough to pull fluorine off the PFAS molecule, a reductive step. A second, oxidizing radical (SO4•−) then stripped away carbon. By alternating these two steps, the process broke the PFAS down completely into simple minerals rather than into smaller fluorinated fragments. The team also built a packed-bed treatment unit (a 'Fenton bed') and report that it treated PFASs efficiently and cheaply in complex, realistic water.
papers.why_it_matters: PFAS contamination of drinking water is widespread and hard to clean up, and destroying the molecules usually costs a lot of energy. A method that fully mineralizes PFAS using only a catalyst and an added chemical could make treatment simpler and cheaper. It also shows that physically confining a reaction in tiny spaces can change which chemical pathways happen.
papers.limitations: The abstract does not give numbers for removal efficiency, cost, which PFAS types were tested, or how long the catalyst stays active, so its performance at real treatment-plant scale remains to be shown.

key_terms.meaning: Human-made chemicals with many carbon–fluorine bonds, used in non-stick and water-repellent products, that persist in the environment.
Complete breakdown of an organic pollutant into simple inorganic products, rather than partial breakdown into other pollutants.
An oxidizing chemical that, when activated by a catalyst, releases highly reactive sulfur-containing radicals.
A catalytic cycle in which a metal (here cobalt) converts an oxidant into reactive radicals that attack pollutants.
A catalyst where the active metal is spread out as individual atoms rather than clumped into particles.
A family of very thin, layered materials made of transition metals combined with carbon or nitrogen.
Running a reaction inside spaces only nanometres wide, which can protect short-lived species and alter reaction pathways.
Removing fluorine atoms from a molecule, the key step in destroying PFAS.

papers.citation: Wang, Y., Zheng, J., Ye, X., Zhou, T., Li, T., Feng, M., Huang, D., Weon, S., Elimelech, M., Wang, X., & Zhang, S. (2026). Steering nanometric reductive-oxidative Fenton-like cycle for PFAS mineralization. Science Advances, 12(47), eaei3786. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aei3786

papers.headline: Simulations suggest modern humans' arrival, not climate alone, doomed Neanderthals
papers.original_title: Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens’ dispersal
papers.reason: Climate-driven agent-based modelling addresses a long-standing debate, finding that the arrival of Homo sapiens, more than climate alone, drove Neanderthal extinction.
papers.summary:
Scientists have long debated whether Neanderthals died out because Europe's climate changed or because Homo sapiens (our species) arrived and competed with them. This study tackled the question with computer modelling. The researchers used climate-driven changes in how suitable the land was for plant-eaters and meat-eaters, along with how much plant growth the land supported, to estimate how many people each region could sustain, how much prey was available, and how much pressure came from competing predators. They fed these map-based estimates into an agent-based model, a simulation in which individual human groups are represented and their populations grow, shrink and move under different scenarios.

In the simulations, shifts in how many people the land could support did not by themselves explain Neanderthals vanishing across Europe as a whole. They did, however, help explain where and when each species lived. Adding Homo sapiens to the picture made Neanderthal extinction much more likely. Because both species went through repeated cycles of population growth and decline, how well-connected their groups were to one another turned out to be the main factor deciding whether populations stayed stable.
papers.why_it_matters: The work suggests that the disappearance of Neanderthals and the spread of modern humans were linked population processes rather than separate events. It also points to contact between groups as a key ingredient for the survival of small, scattered human populations.
papers.limitations: These results come from simulations, so they depend on the assumptions and climate-based estimates built into the model rather than on direct evidence of what happened. The abstract does not say how the conclusions were checked against archaeological data.

key_terms.meaning: The largest population an area can support over time given its food and other resources.
A computer simulation that tracks many individual units (here, human groups) following rules, to see what overall patterns emerge.
How much new plant material an environment produces, which sets the base of the food supply.
Competition and killing among predators that hunt the same prey, such as humans and large carnivores.
How linked separate human groups (bands) are, for example through contact and movement between them.

papers.citation: Vidal-Cordasco, M., Rodríguez-Gómez, G., & Marín-Arroyo, A. B. (2026). Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens’ dispersal. Science Advances, 12(47), eaej5212. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aej5212

papers.headline: Bacteria glide using a protein belt that works like a moving walkway
papers.original_title: Structure and dynamics of the cellular belt driving bacterial gliding motility
papers.reason: A cryo-EM structure plus live imaging reveal the moving 'walkway' belt that powers gliding motility in ecologically and medically important bacteria.
papers.summary:
Some bacteria can move across solid surfaces without flagella or other obvious appendages, a behaviour called gliding motility. In the bacterial group Bacteroidota, which includes both harmless gut residents and disease-causing species, gliding depends on the type IX secretion system (T9SS). This machine exports sticky surface proteins called adhesins, which then travel along a spiral path over the cell body and push the cell forward. The researchers wanted to know what physical structure carries the adhesins along that spiral track.

They isolated the filament responsible for this movement and determined its 3D shape using cryo-electron microscopy. They also filmed living cells. The filament turned out to be a belt made from core parts of the T9SS. It sits in the periplasm, the space between the bacterium's two membranes, and is attached to the outer membrane. Motor proteins of the T9SS drive it. The belt acts like an airport moving walkway, carrying complexes made of an adhesin bound to a barrel-shaped outer-membrane protein. In this way the motors' activity becomes directed motion of the adhesins across the cell surface.
papers.why_it_matters: Bacteroidota are important in many environments, both as harmless partners of animals and as pathogens, so understanding how they move helps explain how they spread and colonise surfaces. The study links two jobs of one machine, secreting proteins and moving them quickly in a set direction within the membrane. This kind of coupling had not been described before.
papers.limitations: The abstract does not say which bacterial species were studied or how widely the findings apply across gliding bacteria. It also does not explain exactly how the motors make the belt move.

key_terms.meaning: Movement of bacteria across a solid surface without swimming appendages such as flagella.
A protein-export machine found in Bacteroidota bacteria that moves proteins to the cell surface.
A surface protein that lets a bacterium stick to a surface or to other cells.
An imaging method in which samples are flash-frozen and viewed with an electron beam, used to work out the 3D structure of large molecules.
The space between the inner and outer membranes of certain bacteria.
A membrane protein folded into a barrel shape that sits in the outer membrane.

papers.citation: Liu, H., Aouizerate, Y., Liu, X., Zhang, Z., Hervada, C. C., Zhu, Y., Vincent, M. S., Cascales, E., Hu, B., & Doan, T. (2026). Structure and dynamics of the cellular belt driving bacterial gliding motility. Science Advances, 12(47), eaef5514. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aef5514

papers.headline: Ordinary graphite helps anode-free sodium batteries charge fast and last long
papers.original_title: Engineering interfacial nucleation and growth for long-life, ultrahigh-rate anode-free sodium batteries
papers.reason: Ampere-hour-scale anode-free sodium pouch cells with stable high-rate cycling, using ordinary graphite, are a practical advance toward cheaper batteries.
papers.summary:
Anode-free sodium batteries skip a separate negative electrode: during charging, sodium metal deposits directly onto a thin metal foil (the current collector), and during discharge it dissolves back off. This saves weight and space, but the deposition and removal tend to be uneven and wasteful, so the batteries lose capacity quickly. The researchers asked whether a common material, graphite, could make this process more controlled and reversible.

They report that graphite does so unexpectedly well. It moves both ions and electrons very quickly, it lets molecules of the ether-based electrolyte solvent slip in and out between its layers reversibly, and its flat, flake-like shape means sodium tends to start growing at the flake edges. Together these effects produce a very thin but sturdy protective film on the surface, which keeps sodium deposition stable at charging rates from 1C to 10C (roughly a full charge in one hour down to about six minutes). Pouch cells holding about one ampere-hour of charge kept 92.3% of the charge on the first cycle and still had 84.9% of their capacity after 1,100 cycles at 3C. They also warmed only slightly at high rates and did not catch fire or overheat uncontrollably when pierced with a nail.
papers.why_it_matters: Sodium is cheaper and more abundant than lithium, and removing the anode can pack more energy into a cell, but poor cycle life has held these designs back. Showing that a cheap, familiar material can steer how sodium metal grows, at practical cell sizes and high charging speeds, points toward low-cost, fast-charging and safer batteries.
papers.limitations: The abstract reports results from laboratory-built pouch cells with a specific ether electrolyte. It does not say how the design behaves under other conditions, at larger scales, or over longer lifetimes than about 1,100 cycles.

key_terms.meaning: A battery built without a pre-made negative electrode; the metal (here sodium) forms directly on a bare current collector during the first charge.
Depositing metal onto a surface while charging (plating) and dissolving it back into the electrolyte while discharging (stripping).
The conductive foil or layer that carries electrons into and out of the electrode.
The first stage of growth, where tiny seeds of new metal begin to form on a surface.
When ions slip between graphite's layers together with the solvent molecules attached to them.
A thin film that forms on the electrode surface from electrolyte breakdown; a good one protects the metal while still letting ions pass.
How fast a battery is charged or discharged relative to its capacity; 1C is about one hour, 10C about six minutes.
The fraction of charge put into a battery that you get back out in the same cycle.
A self-reinforcing overheating that can lead to fire or explosion.

papers.citation: Xie, C., Zhang, J., Liu, S., Lu, J., Wang, P., Meng, X., Tang, Y., Ji, X., & Wang, H. (2026). Engineering interfacial nucleation and growth for long-life, ultrahigh-rate anode-free sodium batteries. Science Advances, 12(47), eaeh3524. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh3524

papers.headline: Exact formulas for how quark distributions inside protons change with energy
papers.original_title: Four-Loop Nonsinglet Splitting Functions in QCD
papers.reason: The first fully analytic four-loop quark nonsinglet splitting functions sharpen the precision of QCD predictions used at colliders.
papers.summary:
Protons and neutrons are made of quarks and gluons, collectively called partons. How the momentum of a proton is shared among its partons is described by parton distributions, and these distributions shift depending on the energy scale at which the proton is probed. The rules for that shift are set by splitting functions, which describe how one parton can turn into others. This paper calculates these splitting functions at the fourth level of approximation (four loops) in quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the theory of the strong force. It focuses on the 'nonsinglet' part, which tracks differences between quark types rather than the overall mix with gluons.

This is a theoretical calculation, not an experiment. The authors reproduce earlier results that covered only parts of this problem. They also obtain, for the first time, complete exact (analytic) formulas for every nonsinglet piece at this order. From these they derive exact forms of two further quantities, called the virtual and rapidity anomalous dimensions, which are used in techniques that sum up large logarithmic terms in predictions. They also give accurate numerical versions of the splitting functions that are ready for practical use.
papers.why_it_matters: Predictions for particle collisions, such as those at the Large Hadron Collider, depend on knowing how parton distributions change with energy. More precise splitting functions reduce theoretical uncertainty in these predictions, which helps when comparing theory with high-precision measurements.
papers.limitations: The results cover only the nonsinglet sector. The abstract does not report complete exact results for the singlet case, which mixes quarks and gluons.

key_terms.meaning: Functions describing how likely it is to find a quark or gluon carrying a given fraction of a proton's momentum.
Quantities that describe how partons branch into other partons, setting how parton distributions change with energy scale.
The fourth level of refinement in a step-by-step approximation (perturbation theory). Each level adds smaller corrections and requires much harder calculations.
Combinations of quark distributions, such as differences between quark flavours, whose evolution does not mix with gluons.
Approximating strong-force calculations as a series of increasingly small corrections.
Numbers that control how quantities change with energy scale. Here, the virtual and rapidity types feed into resummation.
A method that adds up large logarithmic terms to all orders so that predictions stay reliable.

papers.citation: Gehrmann, T., Manteuffel, A. v., Sotnikov, V., & Yang, T. (2026). Four-Loop Nonsinglet Splitting Functions in QCD. Physical Review Letters, 137(21), 211901. https://doi.org/10.1103/sgtd-c4zg

papers.headline: Sending a message through a brick wall using gravity
papers.reason: An experiment demonstrates the novel idea of sending a message through a brick wall using gravitational signals from a moving mass, an essentially unblockable channel.
papers.summary:
Almost all wireless communication, from Wi-Fi to radio, relies on electromagnetic waves. These signals can be shielded or blocked by walls, metal or other obstacles, so they may not get through in difficult environments. The researchers asked whether information could instead travel through a channel that nothing can block, and they proposed gravity. Every mass pulls on every other mass, and no known material screens out that pull.

They designed and built a simple system to test the idea. A sender encodes a message in binary (a string of 0s and 1s) by moving a mass. A receiver uses a gravimeter, a very sensitive instrument that measures tiny changes in gravitational pull, to pick up the resulting changes and decode the bits. In a lab experiment, they sent a message about 0.7 meters through a brick wall at a speed of one bit per minute.
papers.why_it_matters: This experiment shows that gravity can carry information under realistic conditions, giving a communication route that walls and shielding cannot stop. A channel like this could be useful where ordinary radio signals are unreliable or blocked.
papers.limitations: This is a first demonstration over a short distance, under a meter, and at a very slow rate of one bit per minute. The abstract does not say how the method might scale to longer distances or faster speeds.

key_terms.meaning: Waves of electric and magnetic fields, such as radio waves and light, that carry most wireless communication today.
An instrument that measures very small changes in the strength of gravity at a location.
Information written as a sequence of two symbols, usually 0 and 1, each called a bit.
How many bits of information are sent per unit of time. Here it was one bit per minute.

papers.citation: Groszek, A. J., Woffinden, C. W., Harvey, M. D., White, A. G., & Davis, M. J. (2026). Unblockable communication with gravity. Science Advances, 12(47), eaee0802. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aee0802
